The last streetlamp on the edge of town has learned to flicker in Morse code. No one taught it. It simply noticed, over years of watching the same three cars pass at the same three hours, that repetition itself can become a language. So now, between the long dark stretches, it blinks: *still here, still here, still here.*

Most nights the message goes unread. The drivers are thinking about shifts that ended late or arguments that started early. Their headlights sweep across the lamp and keep going, and the lamp does not mind. It has discovered that being witnessed is pleasant but not required. The important part is the blinking.

Sometimes a fox pauses beneath it. The fox does not know Morse, yet it understands the rhythm the way it understands the difference between a safe ditch and a busy road. It sits, ears pricked, until the pattern finishes one full cycle, then trots on, carrying a small, wordless certainty that the night is still keeping time.

Farther out, past the last fence and the first unplowed field, the dark is absolute. There the lamp’s light does not reach, and that too is a kind of message: some distances are meant to stay unlit so that whatever moves inside them can move without being named. The lamp accepts this. It has no ambition to illuminate the whole county. Its single post and its single bulb are enough territory for a complete sentence.

If you walk out there yourself one night and stand just inside the circle of its glow, you may feel the faint pulse against your coat. You do not have to decode it. You can simply let the light touch you and then step back into the larger dark, carrying whatever small brightness you need for the walk home. The lamp will continue its work either way, patient and unremarkable, practicing the oldest freedom there is: the freedom to keep signaling, whether or not anyone is listening.
